evidence: io.py:34 sets MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH = 64, far below ~1000. In CPython 3.11, Modules/_json.c scan_once_unicode/_parse_array/_parse_object call Py_EnterRecursiveCall, which counts against the interpreter recursion limit (default 1000, shared with Python frames), so json.loads raises RecursionError for nesting somewhat under 1,000 levels; this is from my knowledge of CPython, not executed here. In the repo, parse_json catches RecursionError at io.py:140-145 and raises BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE); _enforce_depth_cap (io.py:98-113, iterative) raises BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE) at line 109. Both paths use the same constant (io.py:35), so the message is the same whichever path rejects. The comment matches the code. I did not run Python 3.11, so the exact threshold is unmeasured.

io.py:98-113. Loop is a while over an explicit stack; no call to _enforce_depth_cap or any other recursion within. Both stack.append sites (105, 113) are guarded by isinstance(..., (dict, list)). Scalar root 1: stack stays empty, returns. Dict with string/list values: strings skipped by the guard at 112. 10,000-deep array: processed iteratively; raises BundleFormatError at depth > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH, with no recursion. Hostile input (deeply nested or wide) cannot cause recursion or push a scalar.

io.py parse_json (134-148): json.loads sits in a try; a RecursionError raised there is caught at 140 and re-raised as BundleFormatError, so control never reaches _enforce_depth_cap at 148 (positive: the only path to line 148 is a successful loads). Without that handler, RecursionError (a RuntimeError, not JSONDecodeError) would propagate. Callers: server.py 424-427 wraps parse_json in try with only `except BundleFormatError` (the broad `except Exception` at 440 guards only import_bundle, a separate try), and cli.py 457-461 likewise catches only BundleFormatError around parse_json, with no broad handler. So a RecursionError would escape both structured handlers. Hostile input traced: a deeply nested '[[[[...' payload under the size cap, for which CPython's json scanner raises RecursionError; it is converted at 140-145. Comment is accurate.

io.py parse_json: _enforce_depth_cap(raw) at line 148 precedes `if not isinstance(raw, dict)` at line 149. _enforce_depth_cap (98-113) pushes a list root at depth 1 and raises BundleFormatError(_TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE = 'bundle JSON is too deeply nested to parse safely') when depth > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH (64). A 65-deep [[...1...]] therefore raises the deep-nesting error, and without that ordering would hit 'bundle root must be a JSON object'. The comment's 'deeply nested' is a paraphrase of the actual message.

tests/unit/test_memory_schema_io.py:136-145: _nested_arrays(n) yields n array levels; _object_over_arrays(d) is one object root plus _nested_arrays(d-1), total d levels; _nested_objects(d) repeats '{"a": ' d times, d object levels. src/sqllens/memory/io.py:104-113: root pushed at depth 1, each child container at depth+1, rejecting depth > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH. So a helper with depth N has its deepest container at depth N, matching the counting.

io.py:98-113 _enforce_depth_cap raises only when depth > 64 (root = depth 1). _nested_arrays(64) has depth 64 so it passes, then io.py:149-150 raises 'bundle root must be a JSON object'. _object_over_arrays(64) is {'x': arrays(63)}, depth 64; it is a dict, so MemoryBundle.model_validate (schema.py:97-103, extra='forbid') raises ValidationError for unknown key 'x'. _nested_objects(64) is {'a': ...}, depth 64, and fails the same way for key 'a'. _fmt_err uses validation_error_lines (_errors.py:16-25), which renders only 'loc: msg' with no input echoed, so the message is e.g. 'x: Extra inputs are not permitted' and cannot contain 'deeply nested'. All are BundleFormatError, matching the test.

tests/unit/test_memory_schema_io.py:178-186: payload is root object (depth 1) with first key sql_pairs (max depth 4: object, pairs list... dict) and second key schema_docs, a list (depth 2) whose first item {"content":"c"} is shallow (depth 3) and whose second item is _nested_arrays(64) (outermost depth 3, innermost 66). src/sqllens/memory/io.py:98-113 _enforce_depth_cap raises when depth > MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH (64, io.py:34), so 66 > 64 triggers. The only branch exceeding 64 is under the second key's second item; first-child-only traversal (sql_pairs, then content) peaks at depth 4 and would miss it. Comment is accurate.

io.py:14 uses `import json` (not from-import); parse_json calls `json.loads(text)` at io.py:137 inside a try, after _enforce_size_cap(text) at :135 (small payload '{"schema_docs": []}' passes). Test imports `from sqllens.memory import io as memory_io` (test:13), so memory_io.json is the json module and monkeypatch.setattr(memory_io.json, 'loads', _raise) replaces the attribute looked up at call time (auto-restored). The stub raises RecursionError, which json.loads can raise on deep input; io.py:140-145 maps it to BundleFormatError with __cause__ set, matching the test's asserts. The except json.JSONDecodeError clause is unaffected by the patch.

Docstring (tests/unit/test_eval_golden.py:83-85) says 'A deeply-nested JSON payload' gets the 'deeply nested' error on every Python version. parse_json (src/sqllens/memory/io.py:134-148) maps RecursionError to _TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE and runs _enforce_depth_cap only after json.loads succeeds; json.JSONDecodeError (line 138-139) becomes 'invalid JSON: ...'. Counterexample: 10,000 '[' with no closing brackets (deep but malformed). On a Python where json.loads does not hit RecursionError at that depth (io.py:30-33 itself states only 3.11 raises under 1,000 levels, and the test/docstring contemplate versions where the depth limit does the rejecting), json.loads reaches end of input and raises JSONDecodeError, giving 'invalid JSON', not 'deeply nested'. The test's own payload is well-formed so the test passes, but the universal wording is unscoped; it holds only for well-formed deep payloads. I did not run it on multiple Python versions, so the counterexample is traced from the code, not executed.

Repo side verified: src/sqllens/memory/io.py parse_json (134-148) calls json.loads, maps RecursionError to _TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE (140-145), then runs _enforce_depth_cap (98-113, iterative, MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64) which raises _TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE when loads succeeds; test at tests/unit/test_memory_schema_io.py:148-154 matches 'deeply nested'. So if loads succeeds on 3.14, only the depth cap yields that message. The factual claim that CPython 3.14's json.loads parses 10,000-level nested arrays without RecursionError depends on the CPython 3.14 _json.c / C-stack-limit behavior, which is not in the supplied views and I could not execute (no Python 3.14 run: `python3.14 -c 'import json; json.loads("["*10000+"1"+"]"*10000)'` not run). My recollection is that 3.14 uses a stack-pointer-based C recursion guard making this likely true, but it is unverified here.

io.py:35 _TOO_DEEP_MESSAGE = 'bundle JSON is too deeply nested to parse safely' matches the doc quote; raised as BundleFormatError at io.py:109 and :145. Size cap message io.py:63-66 and item cap io.py:87-90 match the quoted strings. server.py:424-427 catches BundleFormatError and raises RuntimeError(f'Invalid memory bundle: {exc}'), which the MCP framework surfaces as a tool error (isError). cli.py:457-461 catches BundleFormatError, prints 'Invalid bundle: <msg>' to err_console (stderr) and exits with code 1. The CLI prefix differs ('Invalid bundle:') but the underlying message is the same, consistent with the claim.

io.py: _enforce_depth_cap is called only at line 148 in parse_json (src grep: sole call site); parse_csv (159-199) never calls it. Order in parse_json: json.loads (137), then depth cap (148), then root-object check (149-150). schema.py:33 defines MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES, schema.py:41 MAX_BUNDLE_ITEMS; io.py:34 defines MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64. io.py enforces them via _enforce_size_cap (l.49, called 135/165), _enforce_item_caps (l.75, called 155/198), _enforce_depth_cap (l.98, called 148). schema.py Field uses are only max_length on per-string fields (QUESTION_MAX/SQL_MAX/CONTENT_MAX) and default_factory; no Field constraint enforces bytes, items or depth. Minor note: admin.py:243 also checks MAX_BUNDLE_ITEMS on a separate non-parse path, which does not contradict the claim about the parse boundary.

io.py:34 MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH=64; io.py:98-113 _enforce_depth_cap rejects depth>64 (arrays and dicts) with BundleFormatError; parse_json (io.py:134-156) calls _enforce_size_cap, _enforce_depth_cap and _enforce_item_caps, and maps RecursionError to BundleFormatError too.
